quote: Klein's Problem der [-...-] Entstehung von Wirbeln, mittelst des eingetauchten Kaffeelöffels.
english: Klein's problem of the generation of vortices by means of the immersed coffee spoon.
topic: Notes on the analogy between curvature lines in surface theory and distortion lines in continuum mechanics, a remark on the velocity of rest points in a linear continuum, and Klein's problem of how a dipped coffee spoon generates vortices.

triage.modern_statement: This is a known problem in classical hydrodynamics, not a pure-mathematics conjecture. For an ideal (inviscid, incompressible, barotropic) fluid, the Helmholtz/Kelvin vortex theorems say that vorticity cannot be created or destroyed inside the fluid: a flow that starts from rest stays irrotational. Yet if you push a coffee spoon, partly immersed, through a fluid at rest, you can see a pair of vortices form. The question is how to square the two. Can vortices arise in a frictionless fluid when an immersed body moves through it, for example through a surface of discontinuity (a vortex sheet) shed from the body's sharp edges, or through boundary and free-surface effects? Or does explaining the effect require viscosity, as in Prandtl's boundary-layer theory?
triage.answered_by: Felix Klein took up the problem himself in a short 1910 paper, 'Über die Bildung von Wirbeln in reibungslosen Flüssigkeiten' (Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik). Ludwig Prandtl later treated it in 'Über die Entstehung von Wirbeln in der idealen Flüssigkeit, mit Anwendung auf die Tragflügeltheorie und andere Aufgaben' (reprinted in his Gesammelte Abhandlungen). The accepted resolution is that vorticity enters the fluid at boundaries, as vortex sheets shed from sharp edges or through thin viscous layers. Strictly, this resolves a physical paradox rather than settling a formal mathematical problem, which is why confidence is only medium. Modern work cites Klein (1910) on related questions, such as topological sources of vorticity where interfaces meet boundaries.

evidence.claim: Historians of the Göttingen school list the creation of vorticity in ideal fluids, known as 'Klein's Kaffeelöffelexperiment', as one of the notorious fluid-mechanics problems debated there, with the reference Klein (1910).

Eckert's book says that in Klein's seminar the possibility of creating vortices in a frictionless fluid was discussed (as the 'Kaffeelöffelexperiment von Helmholtz'). Two years later Klein gave a short article in the Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik the title 'Über die Bildung von Wirbeln in reibungslosen Flüssigkeiten', and the experiment stayed a much-discussed topic afterwards.

Prandtl's paper on how vortices arise in an ideal fluid starts from the fact that rotation can neither arise nor vanish inside an ideal fluid. It then explains how vortices form anyway, with applications to wing theory.
The Klein 1910 paper is cited in the literature on free and bound vortices in flow fields.

A 2015 JFM paper citing Klein (1910) shows that topological sources of vorticity are present wherever a fluid interface meets horizontal boundaries. Klein's question therefore still feeds current research on how vorticity is generated.
Starting and stopping a spoon in tea or coffee is still used as the everyday motivation for modern experimental and numerical studies of vortex rings made by a translating disk.

triage.why: Hilbert's note clearly refers to Felix Klein's well-known 'Kaffeelöffelexperiment', the paradox of vortex creation in an inviscid fluid, which was debated in Klein's Göttingen seminars. Klein published on it himself in 1910, and Prandtl dealt with it in his work on vortex formation in ideal fluids. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is better described as a classic physical paradox, explained by vortex-sheet shedding from sharp edges and by boundary or viscous-layer effects, than as a formal open problem. How vorticity is generated at boundaries and interfaces is still an active research area, and modern papers cite Klein (1910). I could not confirm the exact date of the seminar discussion or the exact year of Prandtl's paper with the searches available.
